Which document to write: the one-pager, the PRD, the spec and the strategy memo

A product manager's artefacts are not containers for information. Each one is a request for a particular decision from a particular group of people. Choose the wrong artefact and the decision never gets made — however good the writing.

IForty minutes, and no decision

On Tuesday 3 March 2026, Meera Sundaram sat in the executive committee room at Keshanvi Commerce Cloud in Bengaluru and watched a document she had spent three weeks on fail in a way she had not anticipated. It was not rejected. It was simply not used.

Keshanvi sells store-operations software — inventory, billing, shrinkage control, staff rostering — to Indian retail chains. Its revenue run rate was about ₹186 crore, it employed roughly 420 people, and its product organisation had spent two years building depth in grocery and fashion. Meera, a group product manager with eleven years behind her, had spent the winter on a new idea: extending the platform into pharmacy chains, where batch-level expiry tracking and drug recalls make returns management genuinely hard and where the incumbent tools are old. Two prospects had been circling. The engineering commitment she wanted was fourteen engineers for two quarters of FY27, which the finance team costed at roughly ₹4.2 crore fully loaded.

On 18 February she had circulated a twenty-six-page product requirements document titled Pharmacy Vertical: Returns and Recall Management. It was, by any craft standard, a good one. It had user personas for the pharmacist and the chain's quality head, seventeen numbered requirements, a data model for batch lineage, edge cases for partial returns and for stock already dispensed, a telemetry plan, and a phased release outline. Fourteen people were on the distribution list.

The committee spent forty minutes on it. Rohit Deshmukh, the chief financial officer, asked the question that ended the meeting: "Before we discuss returns — are we entering pharmacy at all? Because if we are, this is a three-year commitment with a different compliance surface and a different sales motion, and I have not seen that argument." Meera's document did not contain that argument. It had assumed it. The item was deferred to the April committee, six weeks of engineering planning slipped, and one of the two prospects went quiet.

Nothing in the document was wrong. Meera had simply written the artefact her job title suggested rather than the artefact the decision required. That distinction — and the small set of rules that make it operational — is the subject of this page.

IIThe idea: an artefact is a decision request

Start with definitions, because these four words are used loosely and the looseness is where the damage happens.

A strategy memo (also called a strategy doc or narrative memo) is a written argument for a choice about where to compete and why, including the options not taken. Its audience is whoever controls the allocation of money and people. Its output is a commitment or a refusal.

A one-pager (variously opportunity brief, pitch, problem brief) is a compressed case for spending a bounded amount of effort on one specific problem. Its audience is a small group who can say "go and find out". Its output is permission to proceed to the next stage, usually with a defined budget of weeks.

A PRD — product requirements document — states what is being built, for whom, what will be true after it ships that is not true today, and how the team will know. Its audience is everyone who must act: engineering, design, quality, support, sales enablement, legal. Its output is a shared, inspectable definition of scope that lets many people work in parallel without negotiating with each other every day.

A spec — used here to mean functional specification, including acceptance criteria — states exactly how the system behaves in every case that matters, including the ugly ones. Its audience is implementers and testers. Its output is correctness: two people reading it should build and verify the same thing.

These forms have separate parentage. The requirements document descends from defence and aerospace contracting, where a written specification was literally the contract; the lineage runs through standards such as MIL-STD-490 in the late 1960s and the IEEE's software requirements specification standard, IEEE 830, first issued in 1984 and revised in 1998. The PRD as a distinct product-management artefact emerged in the packaged-software and hardware world of the 1980s and 1990s, where it was deliberately separated from the marketing requirements document so that the question "what shall we build" was answered apart from "what shall we sell". The narrative memo has a different ancestry: Amazon's decision in 2004 to ban presentation slides from senior meetings in favour of six-page prose documents rested on the claim that prose exposes weak reasoning that bullets conceal. The one-pager and its cousins are more recent and more informal — an anti-body that product organisations grew in the 2010s against the discovery of how expensive full requirements documents are when the idea turns out to be wrong.

The sentence Meera could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib is this: the document you write is determined by the decision that is outstanding and the people who must make it, not by the stage of the project or the seniority of the room.

IIIHow it actually works: the ladder and the gates

The four artefacts form a ladder. Each rung assumes the rung above it has been settled and authorises the rung below it. A PRD that is doing its job takes strategic direction as given; a spec that is doing its job takes scope as given. When a document has to argue a question that belongs one rung higher, it stops functioning as that kind of document — which is exactly what happened on 3 March.

The selection procedure has four questions, and practitioners usually leave the second and fourth implicit.

First, what decision is outstanding? Write the decision as a sentence with a verb and an owner: "Rohit and the committee decide whether Keshanvi commits FY27 capacity to pharmacy." If you cannot write that sentence, you are not ready to write anything; you are ready to go and find out who is actually blocked.

Second, who must act, and what will they do differently on the morning after they read it? This is the question that is skipped. A strategy memo changes what the committee funds. A one-pager changes what three people spend the next six weeks on. A PRD changes what nine engineers, two designers and a support lead do all quarter. A spec changes what a tester writes. If nobody's Monday changes, the document has no job.

Third, how reversible is the decision? Jeff Bezos's 1997 letter to Amazon shareholders drew the now-standard distinction between one-way doors, which are costly or impossible to walk back, and two-way doors, which are cheap to undo. Entering pharmacy is close to a one-way door: it changes the compliance surface, the sales motion and two years of roadmap. Changing the default sort order of a returns queue is a two-way door. You owe a one-way door a real argument with alternatives. You owe a two-way door a paragraph and an experiment.

Fourth, what does the document cost in reader-time, and is that proportionate? Almost everyone estimates the cost of writing and almost nobody estimates the cost of reading — which, as the arithmetic below shows, is usually the larger number.

IVA worked example: what twenty-six pages actually cost

Meera's finance partner helped her put numbers on the February document. Keshanvi's blended loaded cost for the people involved was about ₹4,800 per hour. Careful reading of a dense product document runs at roughly six pages an hour — faster if you are skimming, but skimming is precisely what you do not want from a decision-maker. Drafting, including two revision rounds and contributions from a designer and a solution architect, took about 1.5 hours per finished page.

Exhibit 1 — The cost of the February PRD, and what it bought

Two things stand out. The first is that reader-hours (60.7) exceeded author-hours (39.0) by more than half again. The intuition that a document is cheap because "I'll just write it up" is wrong in any organisation with a distribution list longer than five people. The second is the last line. A little over ₹5 lakh is entirely defensible against a ₹4.2 crore commitment — about 1.2 per cent — provided it closes the decision. It closed nothing, because the decision it was shaped to close ("what shall we build in pharmacy?") was not the decision that was open ("shall we be in pharmacy?").

Now run the same arithmetic on the sequence Meera should have written: a three-page strategy memo laying out three options — enter directly, partner with an existing pharmacy-software vendor, or decline for now — with a recommendation; then, if the answer is yes, a one-page brief for the first slice; then a PRD scoped only to that slice, which comes out at nine pages rather than twenty-six because it no longer has to justify anything.

Now change one input and watch the answer move. Suppose Keshanvi's chief executive, not the committee, has the authority to commit a new vertical. The memo's audience collapses from nine readers to one. The arithmetic becomes trivially cheap: eleven author-hours, half a reader-hour, an hour of conversation — about ₹60,000. But the total cost of the decision does not fall, it relocates. A single yes does not tell the sales leadership what to stop selling, does not tell support what to staff, and does not tell the platform team what to keep compatible. Those twenty-odd people now need an artefact of their own — a readout, a written decision record — costing perhaps three hours each, or roughly ₹2.88 lakh of audience time.

The lesson is not that fewer readers are better. It is that the number of people who must change behaviour is the real driver of artefact cost, and it does not disappear when you shorten the distribution list. It merely moves to a second document you have not budgeted for.

VThe nuances that separate understanding from vocabulary

A PRD is not a longer one-pager

The most common confusion treats these four artefacts as points on a single length scale, as though a one-pager grows into a PRD which grows into a spec. They differ in altitude, not length. A one-pager and a PRD about the same feature answer different questions: one asks whether the problem deserves effort, the other assumes it does and defines the solution's boundaries. You can write a two-page PRD and a three-page one-pager without either being wrong. Length is a symptom; altitude is the variable.

"Spec" means at least three different things

In most organisations the word is overloaded: a functional specification describing behaviour, a technical design document describing how the system will be built, and a set of acceptance criteria attached to individual work items. These have different authors — the first is usually the product manager's, the second the engineer's, the third shared. Arguments that appear to be about rigour ("we need a proper spec") are frequently arguments about which of the three is missing. Ask which one, and the disagreement often evaporates.

Documents do not make decisions; owners and meetings do

An artefact's job is to make a decision cheap, well-informed and recorded. It cannot confer authority that does not exist. If the decision has no named owner, the best PRD ever written will circulate, attract comments, and expire. Before writing, find the person whose yes is sufficient. If there is no such person, the outstanding problem is organisational, not editorial.

Reversibility sets the amount of document you owe

A useful rule of thumb: the effort spent on an artefact should scale with the cost of being wrong and the difficulty of reversing, not with the visibility of the project. Teams systematically over-document reversible decisions that happen to be high-profile, and under-document irreversible ones that happen to be dull — schema choices, third-party dependencies, pricing-model commitments.

Snapshots versus living documents

A strategy memo is a snapshot: it is dated, it argues for a choice given what was known then, and it should not be quietly edited afterwards, because its value as a record depends on being fixed. A PRD is a living document, amended as scope changes, with the change visible. A spec should be versioned alongside the code it describes and is ideally expressed so that tests can be derived from it. Treating a memo as living destroys the audit trail of why a decision was made; treating a PRD as a snapshot means it becomes untrue within a fortnight and people stop reading it.

Templates are compressed memory, not judgement

A good PRD template encodes the questions a particular organisation has learned to ask — Keshanvi's includes a section on multi-store data migration because it was burned once. Templates are valuable and worth keeping. But no template can tell you which document to write, and a template followed as a checklist produces documents with well-filled sections and no argument. The first line of any template should be the decision the document is requesting.

Ask what happens if nobody reads it

The default outcome shapes the artefact. If the default is "nothing happens" — as with a new investment — the document must persuade. If the default is "we ship whatever the team builds", the document must constrain. A PRD written in persuasive register when the team is already building is wasted; a persuasive memo written when the default is "no" but phrased as a status update will simply be filed.

What none of these artefacts can tell you

No document can tell you whether the underlying idea is good. A beautifully argued memo for a bad bet reads exactly like a beautifully argued memo for a good one; that is the whole difficulty. Artefacts improve the quality of the decision process — they surface assumptions, force alternatives into the open, and create a record you can learn from later. They do not substitute for evidence from customers. The thoughtful newcomer's question before relying on any of them is: what would I have to observe in the world to change this document's conclusion, and have I gone and looked?

VIHow this differs by product type and company stage

The ladder is stable across contexts; the weight given to each rung is not. At Kethika Learning, a consumer study-app business in Pune, most decisions are two-way doors: a change to the streak mechanic can be run as an experiment on five per cent of users and reversed in a day. There, the dominant artefacts are one-pagers and experiment briefs, PRDs are thin, and much of what would elsewhere be a spec lives in the design file and the analytics event dictionary. Writing a twenty-page PRD for a consumer experiment is not rigour; it is a category error, because the experiment itself is cheaper than the document.

Business-to-business is different in one decisive respect: things get sold before they get built. At Keshanvi, an account team has already told a prospect something. The PRD therefore carries contractual weight, and its most important section is what the product will not do — because in the absence of that sentence, the account team will assume the generous reading. B2B PRDs also acquire readers who never appear on consumer ones: implementation consultants, a customer-success lead, and sometimes the customer's own IT team.

Marketplaces impose a structural discipline. At Kethan Bazaar, a construction-materials marketplace in Ahmedabad, every artefact has to name which side of the market changes behaviour and what happens to the other side while it does. A one-pager that describes only a supplier-side change is not short; it is incomplete, because supply-side changes alter buyer experience with a lag that the document never mentions. The habit of writing "buyer side: no change expected in the first four weeks, then X" is what separates competent marketplace artefacts from generic ones.

In regulated products the spec changes role entirely. At Keshini Money, a lending platform in Mumbai, the specification for how interest is computed and disclosed is not merely an instruction to engineers; it is evidence produced for auditors and, potentially, for a regulator. That means sign-off, versioning and traceability from requirement to test are not bureaucratic overhead — they are the artefact's primary purpose, and the product manager who treats them as friction will discover this at the worst moment.

Stage matters in a way that is often mis-stated. It is not that small companies need fewer documents because they are agile. It is that in a twelve-person company the strategy memo is a conversation over lunch that everyone attends, and the artefact adds little. At 420 people, the memo is the only mechanism by which someone in the Chennai support office learns what the company decided and why. Document weight should scale with the number of people who must act without ever speaking to you.

VIIFour common mistakes and their cheapest diagnostics

Writing a PRD to obtain permission. The symptom, observable from outside, is a PRD with a market-sizing section and a competitive landscape near the front. The underlying misunderstanding is that the PRD is the document that gets you funded; it is the document that coordinates people after you are funded. The diagnostic costs thirty seconds: ask the author, "if this is approved tomorrow, who does something different?" If the honest answer is "we would start the work", the document should have been a memo or a one-pager.

The spec-shaped PRD. The symptom is engineers quietly rewriting the document as tickets, or a designer complaining that the PRD "already designed it". The misunderstanding is that precision about interface details equals rigour. The diagnostic: count how many sentences in the document would have to change if the design team chose a different layout. If it is more than a handful, the PRD has descended a rung and will now go stale every time design iterates.

The strategy memo with no rejected option. The symptom is a nine-page document that reads as advocacy and contains no option B. The misunderstanding is that confidence persuades. In fact a decision-maker cannot commit to a one-way door without knowing what is being given up. The diagnostic is a single question in review: "which option did we not pick, and what would make us switch?" If the author has no answer, the memo is a press release.

Artefact inflation by seniority. The symptom is that document length correlates with the seniority of the audience rather than with the complexity of the decision. The misunderstanding is that length signals seriousness; senior readers have the least time and read the most carefully, so the correlation should run the other way. The diagnostic is the arithmetic in Exhibit 1: compute the reader-hours you are requesting and say the number out loud before sending.

VIIIWhat good looks like

Handled well, Meera's February would have looked like this. On 3 February she writes a three-page memo whose first line is the decision being requested and whose owner is named: "Requested: committee decides by 17 February whether Keshanvi commits FY27 capacity to pharmacy retail." Three options are laid out — enter directly, partner, decline — each with what it costs, what it forecloses, and the two facts that would flip the recommendation. The recommendation is explicit and the uncertainty is stated rather than hidden. Fourteen people are not on the list; nine are, and four of those are told they need only read the first page.

The committee says yes with a condition: prove the recall-reconciliation claim with one chain before more capacity is released. Meera writes a one-page brief for a six-week slice, gets four people, and comes back with evidence. Only then does she write a PRD — nine pages, scoped to the slice, opening with what is out of scope, ending with the telemetry that will tell everyone whether it worked. The specification for batch-lineage behaviour is written jointly with the engineer who will build it and lives next to the tests. Four documents, each answering its own question, totalling thirteen pages, and every one of them closes a decision within a fortnight of being circulated.

IXWhat Meera decided

On 6 March, Meera withdrew the PRD rather than defending it. She wrote a three-page memo titled Pharmacy: enter, partner, or decline, sent it to nine people with a decision date, and got a conditional yes on 17 March — five weeks earlier than the April committee would have produced. Her reasoning, recorded in the memo itself, was that the twenty-six pages had not been wasted; they had been written at the wrong altitude, and about eight of those pages would survive into the eventual PRD once the gate above them had been closed.

The natural next steps are the two artefacts she used most: the discipline of writing a one-pager, which is harder than it sounds because compression is where the argument gets tested, and PRD structure, which is where the question shifts from "which document" to "what belongs in it and in what order". Both assume what this page has argued: that you already know which document the decision requires.

Two questions to sit with. First: think of the last substantial document you wrote at work — can you name the person whose decision it was requesting, and did they make it? Second: in your organisation, which decisions are being made with no artefact at all, and would anyone be able to reconstruct in a year's time why they were made that way?

Module: Requirements & Specification. Builds on: what a product manager does — artefacts are how the role communicates decisions. Unlocks: writing a one-pager; PRD structure.

Which document for which decision: a working theory of product artefacts

The choice between a memo, a one-pager, a PRD and a specification is not a matter of house style. It is a judgement about where the residual uncertainty sits, who bears the cost of ambiguity, and how expensive it is to be wrong. Competent practitioners write well. Experts write the right thing.

ITwo rooms, two documents, one question

On Thursday 22 January 2026, Vikram Raghunathan, vice-president of product at Kethaki Health Systems in Chennai, had a fourteen-page document open and a problem he could not name. Kethaki builds clinical information systems for hospital chains — order entry, nursing charts, discharge workflows — and runs in about 90 hospitals across southern and western India. Revenue was roughly ₹240 crore. The document described an assistive feature: a large language model that drafts the discharge summary from the patient's chart, which the treating physician then edits and signs.

The commercial case was strong. A hospital group with 11 facilities had put ₹11 crore of three-year contract value on the table, conditional on the feature shipping by August. Kethaki's own timing studies put physician effort at 18 to 26 minutes per discharge summary, with about 2,400 discharges a month across the group; even a 40 per cent reduction returns something like 300 physician-hours a month. Thirty-eight engineers sat behind the decision.

What Vikram could not decide was what to write. His instinct — and his previous eleven years of habit — said PRD. But a PRD assumes the shape of the thing is settled, and three questions were open that a PRD had no place for. Would Kethaki stand behind clinical text it had not written? Under India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, what consent basis covered sending chart data to a model, and did it matter whether the model ran inside the hospital's own infrastructure? And what, exactly, does "correct" mean for a paragraph of prose that is right in substance and wrong in emphasis? Dr. Latha Iyer, Kethaki's chief medical information officer, had written one line in the margin of his draft: "You have specified a workflow. You have not specified what happens when it is wrong."

Two weeks later and 1,500 kilometres north-west, Nidhi Barot faced the mirror image. Nidhi is head of product at Kethan Bazaar, an Ahmedabad marketplace for construction materials — cement, TMT bars, plumbing, tiles — connecting about 6,800 suppliers with builders and contractors. Annualised gross merchandise value was around ₹1,400 crore at a take rate of 3.1 per cent. On 5 February she circulated a fourteen-page PRD for a "verified supplier" programme: documentation checks, a quality-dispute record, a badge in search results, and priority placement.

Her chief executive, Harshad Patel, replied in four lines. "This is a policy, not a feature. If we badge suppliers we are taking a position on who deserves demand. What happens to the 4,100 suppliers who don't qualify, and what happens to our GMV in the ninety days while they leave? Write me the argument, not the screens."

Both product leaders had written a competent document. Both had written the wrong one, in opposite directions: Vikram had written at too low an altitude for a decision whose shape was unsettled; Nidhi had written at too low an altitude for a decision that was really about market structure. The rest of this page is an attempt to make that judgement systematic — and to be honest about the places where serious practitioners still disagree about it.

IIThe idea, its history, and the schools that quarrel about it

Define the four artefacts precisely, because the words are used loosely and the looseness is where the argument hides.

A strategy memo is a written argument for a choice among mutually exclusive courses of action, including those not taken, addressed to the people who control money and headcount. It is a snapshot: dated, argued from what was known then, and valuable afterwards precisely because it is not edited. A one-pager is a compressed case for spending a bounded quantity of effort investigating or building one thing; its output is permission with a budget attached. A product requirements document states what is being built, for whom, what becomes true on release, what is explicitly excluded, and how success will be observed; its output is a shared definition of scope that lets many people work in parallel without renegotiating daily. A specification — meaning here a functional specification with acceptance criteria — states behaviour case by case, including error and boundary cases, at a precision from which tests can be derived.

The lineages are separate and the separation explains the quarrels. Written requirements entered software from defence and aerospace procurement, where the document was the contract: MIL-STD-490 in 1968, then the IEEE's software requirements specification standard, IEEE 830, issued 1984 and revised in 1998, which gave a generation the vocabulary of "shall" statements, completeness, consistency and traceability. Academic requirements engineering deepened it — Michael Jackson's Software Requirements & Specifications (1995) insisting on the distinction between the machine and the world it acts on, Alistair Cockburn's Writing Effective Use Cases (2000), Karl Wiegers's Software Requirements (1999). The PRD is a commercial-software descendant, deliberately separated in the 1980s and 1990s from the marketing requirements document so that "what shall we build" was argued apart from "what shall we sell". The narrative memo has an entirely different parent: Amazon's 2004 replacement of slide decks with six-page prose documents, later extended into the working-backwards press-release-and-FAQ, on the claim that prose exposes weak reasoning that bullets conceal.

Against all of this the Agile Manifesto of 2001 asserted a preference for working software over comprehensive documentation, and Ron Jeffries's three Cs — card, conversation, confirmation — recast the written story as a token for a discussion rather than a record of one. Two more recent schools matter. Ryan Singer's Shape Up (Basecamp, 2019) argued for specifying boundaries rather than interiors: a pitch with a fixed appetite, deliberately coarse "fat marker" sketches, and named rabbit holes and no-gos, leaving design decisions inside the boundary to the team. Marty Cagan's work, from Inspired (2008) to Empowered (2020), went further and treated the PRD-as-handoff as diagnostic of a team that is being told what to build rather than which problem to solve.

Exhibit 1 — Five schools, and the specific propositions each would and would not sign
SchoolWould signWould not signEvidence it rests on
Requirements engineering (IEEE 830, Wiegers, Jackson)Ambiguity resolved late costs far more than ambiguity resolved early; requirements must be testable and traceable"The document is a placeholder for a conversation"Defect-cost studies from large systems; regulated and safety-critical delivery
Narrative memo (Amazon)Prose forces reasoning; sixty silent minutes beats a presented deck"The memo should define system behaviour"Two decades of internal decision quality; no controlled comparison exists

Shaping (Singer, Shape Up)Specify boundaries and appetite; leave the interior to the team"The PM writes acceptance criteria"Cycle-time stability at small, co-located teams
Empowered teams (Cagan)A PRD written to be handed over signals a feature team, not a product team"The PRD is the primary artefact"Comparative practice at high-performing product companies

Each school is internally coherent. They disagree less about writing than about where a company's real uncertainty lies — which is why the same argument recurs unresolved every few years.

The unifying claim this page will defend is narrower than any single school and, being narrower, is compatible with most of them: the artefact you owe is determined by which uncertainty is currently dominant, how many people must act on the answer, and where ambiguity is cheapest to discover. Strategy memos attack uncertainty about whether and why. One-pagers buy information about whether a problem is worth solving. PRDs attack uncertainty about what, across many actors. Specifications attack uncertainty about exactly how, where getting it wrong is expensive to find later.

IIIMechanics in depth, with the arithmetic practitioners skip

Experts make this choice with two calculations, one about the value of a document and one about the cost of ambiguity. Both are crude; both are far better than instinct.

The value of a document. A document is worth writing when the expected value of the decision improvement exceeds its total cost in author-hours and reader-hours. Write it as E = p × ΔV − C, where p is the probability that writing it changes the decision or materially improves its execution, ΔV is the value difference between the outcomes, and C is the fully loaded cost of writing and reading. The term that practitioners consistently underestimate is C, because they count their own hours and not their readers'. At a careful reading rate of about six pages an hour, Nidhi's fourteen-page PRD sent to nineteen people requests roughly 44 reader-hours before anyone speaks. At Kethan Bazaar's blended loaded rate of ₹4,400 an hour that is about ₹1.95 lakh of attention, against the eight author-hours she was mentally accounting for.

The term practitioners overestimate is p. For a decision the organisation has already effectively made, p is near zero and the document is theatre; the honest move is to write a one-paragraph decision record instead. For Nidhi, p was genuinely high: Harshad had not decided, the two options had different three-year shapes, and a written argument would plausibly move him. Take ΔV crudely as the difference between a verified-supplier programme that lifts buyer conversion by 1.2 percentage points on ₹1,400 crore of GMV at 3.1 per cent take rate — about ₹52 lakh of annual revenue — and one that drives away long-tail supply and costs more than it earns. Even at p = 0.3 and a conservative ΔV of ₹1 crore, a memo costing ₹2 lakh is obviously worth writing. The calculation is not the point; the discipline of computing reader-hours before pressing send is.

The cost of ambiguity. The second calculation decides how far down the ladder to go — whether a PRD suffices or a specification is owed. Model expected rework as R = N × q × c, where N is the number of statements in the document that could reasonably be read two ways, q the probability each is in fact misread, and c the cost of discovering and correcting the misreading at the point it surfaces. Compare R with the cost of an additional specification pass.

Read the middle column carefully, because it is the one people refuse to believe. When a team has built the same class of thing three times, q collapses, and the further specification pass destroys value: ₹2.7 lakh spent to avoid ₹1.98 lakh of expected rework. This is the strongest form of the agile objection, and it is arithmetically correct within its domain. The requirements-engineering school is equally correct within the third column. The two schools are not disagreeing about writing; they are working in different columns of the same table and generalising.

Three second-order effects deserve naming, because they are the steps expert practitioners take without articulating them.

The first is the document as a coordination substitute. A PRD's real economic function in an organisation above roughly fifty people is to remove the need for pairwise conversation. Nine engineers, two designers, a support lead and a solutions consultant would otherwise need to reach agreement through roughly seventy-eight pairwise exchanges. The PRD is worth writing when the cost of writing it is less than the cost of those conversations not happening — which is why the same feature genuinely deserves a PRD at Kethaki and does not at a twelve-person startup.

The second is the shelf-life problem. Each artefact decays at a different rate, and the decay rate should determine both its form and where it lives. A strategy memo decays slowly because it records a judgement at a moment; its correctness as a historical record does not decay at all. A specification decays fastest, which is the argument for keeping it adjacent to the code and expressing it so tests can be generated from it. The common pathology is a PRD kept in a document tool, amended nine times in eleven weeks, with no indication of what changed — which is worse than no document, because people act on remembered versions.

The third second-order effect is the authorisation illusion. Writing a document creates the feeling that a decision has been made. It has not; a decision requires an owner who says yes and an organisation that behaves differently afterwards. The test is behavioural: a fortnight after circulation, has anyone's calendar changed?

IVWhen the framework applies, and when it misleads

State the conditions as claims that can be checked rather than as advice.

Claim one: the artefact should match the dominant open uncertainty. Applied to Nidhi, the dominant uncertainty was whether Kethan Bazaar should differentiate supply at all — a question about market structure, not screens; her PRD fails the test. Applied to Vikram, the dominant uncertainty was the behaviour of the system when it errs, which is neither a strategy question nor a scope question but a specification question that nobody had yet enough evidence to answer. His PRD also fails, but for the opposite reason: he needed to descend, not ascend, and first to buy information.

Claim two: the depth of specification should scale with the cost of ambiguity, not with the visibility of the project. Exhibit 2 operationalises it. Kethaki's discharge feature touches a regulated interface — data leaving the hospital's boundary under the DPDP Act's consent framework and records that feed the hospital's accreditation documentation — so the third column governs, and a specification pass is worth roughly eight times its cost. Kethan Bazaar's badge is, technically, a straightforward change to a search ranking and a profile record; the first column does not apply and a heavy spec would be waste.

Claim three: document weight should scale with the number of people who must act without speaking to the author. At Kethaki, thirty-eight engineers across Chennai and a four-person integration team in Pune means the written artefact carries weight no conversation can. Kethan Bazaar's product organisation is nineteen people in one building; much of what Nidhi wrote down would have been settled faster standing up.

Where is the framework actively misleading? In three places. First, when the decision is genuinely exploratory and the honest answer is that nobody knows what the thing is — the artefact discipline can produce confident documents about imaginary products, and a prototype would have cost less and taught more. Second, in organisations where documents function as political instruments; there, artefact choice is rational behaviour aimed at a different objective, and pretending otherwise wastes everyone's time. Third, when the "decision" is really a negotiation between two teams with different incentives. No document resolves a misaligned incentive; it merely records the disagreement in prose, and the most common symptom is a PRD that has been in review for five weeks with 130 comments.

VHard edge cases and what mature companies actually do

Multi-product and platform. When one capability serves three products, the classic failure is two PRDs for one feature: the platform team writes one describing the capability, the product team writes one describing the experience, and the two disagree about defaults. Mature organisations resolve this not by merging the documents but by naming which one owns which decision class. At Kethra Logistics Cloud in Gurugram, the convention is blunt: the platform document owns contracts, limits and failure semantics; the product document owns defaults, copy and the moment of use; and any statement appearing in both is deleted from the product document and cited.

Two-sided markets. Kethan Bazaar's discipline is that no artefact is complete unless it states what happens to the other side, and with what lag. The verified badge changes buyer search results immediately; it changes supplier behaviour over eight to twelve weeks, as unbadged suppliers discover reduced visibility and either invest in qualification or leave. A PRD that describes only the badge is not short — it is false by omission, because it implies the change is bounded.

Regulated products. Here the specification stops being an instruction and becomes evidence. Kethaki's specification for what the system does when a physician rejects a generated summary will, if the feature is ever examined, be read by people who were not in the room: auditors, the hospital's accreditation team, potentially a data-protection authority under the DPDP framework. That changes its properties. It must be versioned, signed off with names and dates, and traceable from requirement to test case. Product managers who treat this as bureaucratic drag are not wrong that it is slow; they are wrong that it is optional.

Hardware plus software. Keshavan Instruments, a Coimbatore maker of patient-monitoring devices that Kethaki integrates with, forces a discipline software teams find alien: a firmware freeze date. Once the freeze passes, changing behaviour costs a field update across installed devices at roughly ₹2,600 per unit in engineer travel and downtime. When part of a system cannot be revised cheaply, specification must precede build for that part — not because of philosophy but because the reversibility assumption underlying "we'll iterate" is false there. The practical pattern in mixed systems is a split artefact: a frozen, formal specification for the device boundary, and a living PRD for the software that surrounds it.

AI-native features. This is where the four-artefact model strains hardest, and Vikram's problem is the general case. A specification in the classical form — given this input, when this happens, then this output — presumes determinism. A model that drafts a discharge summary produces a different paragraph on Tuesday than on Monday, both defensible. What can be specified is not the output but the envelope: the evaluation set and how it was constructed, the acceptable rate and distribution of error classes, what the interface does on low confidence, what is logged, what the human must do before the artefact becomes clinical record, and what is never attempted. Kethaki's eventual working phrase was "specify the behaviour of the system around the model, and the measured envelope of the model itself." The classical spec does not disappear; it moves to the guardrails.

Organisational seams. Artefacts fail most often at boundaries between teams with different planning cycles. The observable symptom is an artefact that has an author but no reader with authority on the other side of the seam.

VINine distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

1. Altitude is not length. The tell is a practitioner who says "I'll write a short PRD" when what is needed is a one-pager. The obvious reading — that these artefacts sit on a continuum of detail — is wrong, because they answer different questions. A two-page PRD and a three-page one-pager are both perfectly ordinary. The expert asks what question is open, then decides how long the answer needs to be.

2. The document's job is to make a decision cheap, not to be complete. The tell is a document that has no requested decision in its first three lines. Experts open with the decision, its owner and its date; everything after is support. The obvious reading — that the document should be a full account of the thinking — mistakes the archive for the instrument.

3. Reader-hours are the real cost. The tell is an author who can state their own hours but not the distribution list's. Once you compute it, distribution-list discipline improves immediately: at Kethaki, the practice of writing "full read: 4 people; first page only: 11" beside the circulation line cut average review load by about a third.

4. Snapshot and living artefacts need different homes. The tell is a strategy memo that has been quietly edited after the decision. The obvious reading is that keeping documents current is virtuous. It is, for PRDs. For memos it destroys the only thing that makes the corpus valuable later: the ability to ask what was known when the bet was placed, which is the raw material of calibration.

5. What is excluded is the most valuable sentence in a business-to-business PRD. The tell is a sales conversation in which a customer describes a capability nobody agreed to. In enterprise sales the generous reading is always adopted downstream, so an unstated exclusion is functionally a promise.

6. "Spec" names at least three artefacts. Functional specification, technical design document, and acceptance criteria have different authors and different readers. The tell is a disagreement framed as "we need more rigour" that dissolves the moment someone asks which of the three is missing.

7. Consensus on a document is not the goal; convergence on a decision is. The tell is a PRD with more than about eighty comments. Past that threshold the document has become a forum, and the expert move is to close comments, list the three open questions, and convene fifteen minutes with the people who can answer them.

8. The artefact cannot validate the idea. The tell is a team that feels more confident after writing than before, with no new evidence in between. Documents improve reasoning about evidence; they manufacture nothing. The expert habit is to write, beside the conclusion, what observation would falsify it — and then to check whether anyone has gone to look.

9. Templates encode memory, not judgement. The tell is a document with every section filled and no argument in any of them. A template is a list of questions an organisation learned to ask after being hurt; it cannot tell you which document to write, and a strong practitioner deletes sections that do not apply and says why in one line.

VIIHow this differs across product types and stages

Exhibit 3 — Where the weight falls, by context
ContextArtefact that carries the weightThe section that matters most
Consumer, reversible changesOne-pager plus experiment briefThe stop rule and the metric guardrails
B2B SaaS with named accountsPRDExplicit exclusions
Enterprise with procurementSpecification, as contractual evidenceTraceability and sign-off
Platform serving internal teamsInterface specificationFailure semantics and limits
Marketplace, two-sidedStrategy memo, then PRDEffect on the other side, and its lag
Hardware plus softwareSplit: frozen spec, living PRDThe freeze date and what it binds
AI-native featuresPRD plus evaluation specificationError envelope and human checkpoint

Where the difference is not real, it should be said plainly: the choice procedure — which uncertainty, how many actors, how reversible — is identical in every row. Only the answers move.

Stage changes the answers more than practitioners admit, and the usual telling of it is wrong. The claim that small companies need fewer documents because they are nimble confuses cause and effect. In a fifteen-person company the strategy memo is a conversation everybody hears, so the written artefact adds little beyond a record; the marginal value of writing is low because the coordination it substitutes for is already free. At Kethaki's 640 people, a decision that is not written down does not exist outside the room it was made in, and a support engineer in Chennai will discover it from a customer. The correct formulation is that artefact weight tracks the number of people who must act correctly without ever speaking to the author, and that number grows roughly with the square of organisational size in the early years before flattening.

VIIIThree worked examples, including one that failed

Example one: Kethan Bazaar's supplier payout change, September 2025 — the failure. Nidhi's team shipped a change to settlement timing off a two-page memo. The memo said payouts would settle at T+1 for verified suppliers instead of T+3. It did not define the cut-off hour, did not say what happened to an order dispatched at 11 p.m., and did not state whether a partially delivered order settled proportionally. The team judged, not unreasonably, that these were details the engineers would sort out. Some 2,100 suppliers were affected. Over nine days the support queue took 1,340 payout disputes; the finance team reconciled by hand at an estimated 640 person-hours; roughly ₹64 lakh of combined support, reconciliation and goodwill credits was spent; and 140 suppliers stopped listing, of whom 96 never returned. The failure was not the memo's brevity. It was that a memo — an artefact for arguing a choice — was used to transmit behaviour to people who had to implement it. The recovery was instructive: not a fourteen-page document, but a one-page behaviour table with eleven rows covering the cases, appended to the memo and versioned with the payout service. Total cost of the recovery artefact, about nine hours.

Example two: Kethaki's probe, February to March 2026. Vikram stopped work on the PRD and wrote a one-page brief instead: six weeks, four people, one question — across 200 real discharge summaries reviewed by three physicians, what fraction of generated drafts are accepted with no edit, with minor edits, with substantive edits, and what classes of error occur. The brief named its stop rule: if substantive edits exceeded 30 per cent, the feature would be re-scoped to a structured-data summariser rather than free prose. The results were 41 per cent accepted with minor edits, 47 per cent with substantive edits, and — the finding that mattered — the substantive edits clustered into three classes, of which one, omission of a medication change made on the final day, was both frequent and clinically serious. That single observation was worth more than the entire fourteen-page PRD, because it converted an unspecifiable problem into a specifiable one: the guardrail is that any medication change within 24 hours of discharge must be surfaced separately and confirmed. Probe cost, roughly ₹19 lakh. Avoided cost, if the feature had shipped with that omission class unhandled, was not calculable but was clearly larger.

Example three: the verified-supplier memo, February 2026. Nidhi replaced the PRD with a four-page memo presenting three options — no differentiation, a badge with priority placement, and a quality-guarantee scheme in which Kethan Bazaar underwrites disputes — with the balance-sheet consequence of each. The third option was the one the PRD had never contemplated and was the one Harshad found most interesting, because it monetised trust directly rather than through ranking. The memo's central exhibit was a simple sensitivity: at a 1.2-point conversion lift the badge earns about ₹52 lakh a year; if the unbadged tail contracts by 12 per cent and takes 6 per cent of GMV with it, the programme loses about ₹2.6 crore of GMV, or roughly ₹80 lakh of revenue. That arithmetic, four lines long, reframed the decision from a product question into a supply-elasticity question the company had never measured — and the outcome of the memo was not a yes or a no but a commissioned two-week measurement.

IXFailure modes, early warnings, and the cost of catching them late

Exhibit 4 — Four failure modes and their diagnostics
Failure modeEarly warning signDiagnostic questionCost if caught at release
PRD used to seek permissionMarket sizing appears on page two"If approved tomorrow, whose Monday changes?"One planning cycle, 4–8 weeks
Memo used to transmit behaviourEngineers ask for "the detail doc""Can a tester derive a test from this sentence?"Rework plus support load (see Example one)
Spec written before the shape is knownAcceptance criteria rewritten twice a week"What have we learned that changed this?"Wasted specification effort and team cynicism
Document as forumMore than 80 comments, five weeks open"Which three questions are actually open?"Decision latency; the option expires

The pattern across all four is that the cost of a misjudged artefact is almost never the paper. It is delay, and delay is priced in lost options: a contract window, a competitor's move, a customer's patience. Kethan Bazaar's payout failure cost ₹64 lakh in cash and rather more in the confidence of 2,100 suppliers. Kethaki's deferred committee decision, in the parallel case of a slipped planning cycle, would have cost a contract window that did not reopen until the next budget year.

XWhere thoughtful people genuinely disagree

Does the cost of a defect really rise by orders of magnitude the later it is found? Barry Boehm's Software Engineering Economics (1981) popularised a curve in which a requirements defect costs many times more to fix in production, and the rough ratios of 1:10:100 became folklore that justifies heavy up-front specification. The steelman for it: in systems with physical deployment, regulatory review, or integration with third parties, a late change genuinely does trigger re-certification, field visits and downstream coordination, and Keshavan Instruments' ₹2,600-per-unit field update is exactly that curve made concrete. The steelman against: Laurent Bossavit's The Leprechauns of Software Engineering (2012) traced the citation chain and found the empirical base far thinner than its confident use implies, drawn from a small number of old, large, non-commercial projects. What would have to be true for the pro-specification position to be wrong? That the marginal cost of change in modern deployment — continuous release, feature flags, reversible migrations — has fallen enough that the curve is nearly flat for most software. That is plainly true for Kethan Bazaar's badge and plainly false for Kethaki's regulated interface. The honest position is that the curve is real but domain-specific, and quoting the ratios without naming the domain is the error.

Is the PRD an anti-pattern or essential infrastructure? The Cagan position, steelmanned: if a product team is empowered to solve a problem, the written requirement describes a solution someone else chose, and its existence proves the team was not trusted with the problem; prototypes and outcome briefs communicate more, faster, and with less staleness. The opposing position, steelmanned: in any organisation where more than about fifteen people must act coherently, and particularly where support, legal and sales must prepare in parallel, the PRD is the cheapest available coordination technology, and calling it an anti-pattern confuses its misuse as a handoff with its use as a shared definition. What would falsify the anti-pattern view? Evidence that large empowered teams coordinate as well without a written scope definition as with one — which nobody has produced, partly because the counterfactual is unobservable.

Should product managers write acceptance criteria? The shaping school says no: the PM sets boundaries and appetite, and the interior is the team's. The requirements school says yes, because acceptance criteria are where intent survives contact with implementation, and delegating them delegates the definition of done. Both are defensible and the disagreement is not resolvable in the abstract; it turns on whether the team's engineers have enough domain context to make those calls. Kethaki's engineers do not know which medication-change omissions are clinically serious; Kethan Bazaar's engineers know perfectly well what a partial delivery is.

Does generative AI make specifications more or less valuable? Since about 2024 this has become the live argument. One camp holds that when code is cheap to generate and regenerate, the durable asset is the specification: a precise statement of intended behaviour becomes the thing worth maintaining, and the PRD moves closer to being executable. The other holds the opposite — that cheap generation makes the prototype cheaper than the document, so exploratory specification is now strictly dominated by building the thing and looking at it. Both camps have a point and they are describing different phases: the second is right during exploration, the first is right once behaviour must be preserved across regenerations. What would settle it is evidence about maintenance, which the field does not yet have.

XIWhat mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this behaves differently in four observable ways. They open by naming the decision, its owner and its date, and will not begin drafting until they can write that sentence — which frequently reveals that no such owner exists, and turns an editorial task into an organisational one. They compute reader-hours before circulating and shape the distribution list accordingly, including telling named people to read only the first page. They can say aloud which uncertainty is dominant right now and will cheerfully abandon a half-written document when the answer changes, as Vikram did. And they treat the corpus as an asset: memos stay frozen so the company can later audit its own reasoning, PRDs carry visible change histories, specifications live beside the code they govern. The person who has merely studied the topic produces better-structured documents. The person who has mastered it produces fewer, shorter ones, and more decisions per quarter.

XIIWhat each protagonist decided

Vikram abandoned the PRD on 27 January and wrote the one-page probe brief instead, arguing to Kethaki's executive team that the company could not scope a feature whose failure modes it had not observed. The probe finished on 11 March. He then wrote two artefacts rather than one: a nine-page PRD for the physician workflow, and a separate, versioned evaluation specification owned jointly with Dr. Iyer defining the error classes, their acceptable rates, the mandatory medication-change confirmation, and the audit log required under the hospital group's data-protection commitments. The August date held, with the scope narrowed to three specialties.

Nidhi withdrew her PRD on 9 February and wrote the four-page memo. Harshad did not choose the badge; he commissioned a two-week measurement of supply elasticity in two cities, on the grounds that the memo had shown the decision turned on a number nobody had. Nidhi's private view, recorded in the memo's appendix and worth more than the decision itself, was that Kethan Bazaar had been making supply-side policy through product features for two years without ever writing the policy down.

Three questions for discussion. First: Vikram's probe cost ₹19 lakh and produced no shipped software — under what circumstances is that a good use of six weeks, and how would you have defended it to a board that measures delivery? Second: Nidhi's memo converted a product decision into a measurement request; is that an act of rigour or an act of delay, and what would distinguish the two in advance? Third: consider an organisation you know well — which of its recurring decisions are made with no artefact at all, and could anyone reconstruct, a year later, why they were made that way?

XIIIGoing deeper

  1. What a product manager does — artefacts are the medium through which the role exercises influence without authority; understanding the role explains why the artefact question is not clerical.
  2. Writing a one-pager — the hardest artefact to write well, because compression is where a weak argument becomes visible; unlocks the discipline of stating an appetite and a stop rule.
  3. PRD structure — once the artefact is chosen, the question becomes what belongs in it and in what order; the section sequence itself encodes a theory of what the reader needs first.
  4. Customer narratives (Day 0 / Day N) — the technique that keeps a PRD honest about the difference between first use and habitual use, which is where most B2B scope errors hide.
  5. Acceptance criteria and error cases — the rung below the PRD, and the place where Kethan Bazaar's payout failure actually occurred.
  6. Telemetry requirements — a claim about success is idle unless the instrumentation to observe it is specified before the build, not after.
  7. Non-functional requirements — latency, availability, retention and privacy obligations rarely fit a user story, and are the most common omission in an otherwise good PRD.
  8. Release criteria and success metrics — the artefact that closes the loop, converting "what changes when it ships" from rhetoric into a threshold someone must sign against.
  9. User stories and epics — the format in which most PRD content is eventually consumed by delivery teams, and the translation step where intent is most often lost.

Module: Requirements & Specification. Learning objective: which document to write for which decision and audience. Builds on: what a product manager does. Unlocks: writing a one-pager; PRD structure.
case20v1-req.artifact.types:
Nirnay Works: Which Document First?

A teaching case on choosing the product artefact for the decision and the audience

1. Opening

At 7.40 on the evening of Tuesday 20 October 2026, Amanpreet Hothi sat in the Pune office of Nirnay Works Private Limited with three messages open on her screen. Hothi, the company's Director of Product, had until noon on Wednesday to decide which document she would write first. Three colleagues had each asked her, within one fortnight, for a different document about the same initiative, a payment-collection feature called Nirnay Collect. She could give about six working days to writing before the engineering planning lock on Friday 30 October. The Dubai client's call fell on Tuesday 27 October, the board met on Thursday 5 November, and Diwali arrived on Sunday 8 November, after which very little would move until the new year. Whichever document she started on Wednesday would decide which of the three people got what they needed first.

2. Company background

Nirnay Works was founded in 2017 in Pune by Arshdeep Hunjan, a chartered accountant who had spent his early career watching wholesale distributors reconcile ledgers by hand. The company sells billing, GST invoicing and credit-ledger software to distributors of FMCG, pharmaceutical and hardware goods, businesses with annual turnover of ₹5 crore to ₹80 crore that supply a few hundred small retailers each. In September 2026 it had 12,000 paying accounts at an average of ₹75,000 a year, annual recurring revenue of ₹90 crore, and about 140 employees. Its eleven engineers worked in Bengaluru (seven) and Pune (four).

The market was crowded. Tally Prime sat on most distributors' desks; Zoho Books and Vyapar competed on price and mobile convenience; Khatabook held the retailer's side of the ledger. Distributors kept asking why an invoice raised in Nirnay could not be paid through UPI, the NPCI network on which their retailers already paid for everything else. Collect was the answer: a UPI payment link and QR code on every invoice, settled through Razorpay as the licensed payment aggregator, with each payment matched to the ledger automatically. Nirnay never held customer money. Because payers' phone numbers and UPI handles now passed through the product, the company also treated the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act as a design constraint from the first sketch.

3. The situation

From 6 July to 27 September 2026, 180 volunteer distributors ran Collect in a pilot. Exhibit 2 gives the results. Hothi's team priced the feature as an add-on at ₹1,500 a month, or ₹18,000 a year. If 4,000 of the 12,000 accounts took it in the first year, it would add ₹7.2 crore, against a build budget of ₹6.4 crore spread over four quarters.

The three requests are set out in Exhibit 1. Hothi had also pulled the time records of the last three initiatives, with the document each had started from (Exhibit 3). Figure 1 shows the dates that bore on her choice. A fourth date lay off the chart: the Dubai client's contract renewal on 31 January 2027.

Figure 1. The three weeks before Diwali, 2026.

The team was spread across time zones, and that shaped how documents were read. The contract designer in Berlin had drawn the payment-link screens but would not start the reconciliation screens until the data fields were fixed in writing; she sat 3.5 hours behind Pune, a gap that widened to 4.5 hours on 25 October, so her day began around Pune's lunchtime. In New Jersey, the sales head sat 9.5 hours behind Pune until 1 November, so calls took place in his morning and Pune's evening. Dubai was only 1.5 hours behind. Anything Hothi wrote would be read, and argued over, asynchronously, by people who could not easily ask what she had meant.

4. The people

Arshdeep Hunjan, chief executive and founder, Pune. He wanted a strategy document. "I cannot ask a board for ₹6.4 crore on the strength of a feature list," he told Hothi. He remembered the 40-page GST filing PRD as one that "nobody outside engineering ever opened".

Anhad Hehar, engineering manager, Bengaluru. He led seven of the eleven engineers and wanted a PRD. The request covered 22 engineer-weeks, and without it by the 30th his team would book the quarter to maintenance. He pointed to the ledger-sharing overrun in Exhibit 3: "Nobody had written down what done meant."

Aarav Hanjra, head of sales for the US and Middle East, New Jersey. He owned the Dubai account: a trading group with 240 Nirnay accounts, worth ₹1.80 crore a year, due for renewal on 31 January 2027. On 12 October he had told the client's finance head that he would "come back with something in writing". He wanted "a spec with a date" for the client's multi-entity reconciliation. The client's own email, which he forwarded, asked for "written confirmation of the expected delivery window before we open renewal talks".

5. Exhibits

The three tables below are discussed in sections 3, 4 and 6.

Exhibit 1. The three requests, as received

RequesterDecision it serves (date)Document asked forWriting days
Arshdeep Hunjan, CEOAsk the board for ₹6.4 crore (5 Nov; papers out 2 Nov)Strategy document4
Anhad Hehar, EngineeringCommit 22 engineer-weeks in the January quarter (30 Oct)PRD6
Aarav Hanjra, SalesWhat to tell the Dubai client (27 Oct)"Spec with a date"3
Total13

Writing days are Hothi's own estimates. The January quarter holds about 132 engineer-weeks (11 engineers × 12 net weeks), so 22 is one-sixth of it.

Exhibit 2. Collect pilot, 180 volunteer accounts, 6 July to 27 September 2026

MeasureValue
Average monthly billing per account₹36 lakh
Receivable days, 12 weeks before pilot47
Receivable days, final four weeks of pilot39
Reduction8 days
Cash released per account (8 days × ₹1.2 lakh daily billing)₹9.6 lakh
Cash released, all 180 accounts₹17.28 crore
Share of invoice value paid through the link61%

Daily billing is ₹36 lakh ÷ 30. Cash released is a one-time improvement in working capital, not an annual figure. The 180 accounts volunteered, no comparison group was run, and the 12-week windows are not adjusted for season.

Exhibit 3. The last three initiatives, by starting document

InitiativeStarting documentPlanned eng-weeksActual eng-weeksOverrun
Bulk GST return filing40-page PRD1820+11.1%
Ledger sharing with retailersOne-page brief1423+64.3%
Hindi voice invoicingStrategy memo, short PRD1215+25.0%
Total / pooled4458+31.8%

Engineer-weeks are from Hehar's team time records. The pooled overrun is total overrun (14) ÷ total planned (44), not the mean of the three rates.

6. The options

Option A: write the PRD first. Six writing days, finishing Wednesday 28 October. It would set out scope, acceptance criteria and data fields for the full 22 engineer-weeks. It commits that capacity before the board has decided on the ₹6.4 crore, and it uses every writing day available.

Option B: write the strategy document first. Four writing days, finishing Monday 26 October, ahead of the board papers on 2 November. It would set out the market, the pilot evidence, the investment and the risks behind the ₹6.4 crore request. It specifies no features, and it leaves two writing days.

Option C: write a one-page brief first. One and a half days, circulated on Thursday 22 October to all three. It would state the problem, the pilot evidence in Exhibit 2, a first slice of 8 engineer-weeks inside the quarter, and the decision it asks of each reader. About four and a half writing days would remain, and it replaces neither a strategy document nor a PRD.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. What decision does each of the three requesters have to take, by when, and what must they see to take it?
  2. What can Exhibit 3 tell Hothi about the link between starting document and overrun, and what can it not?
  3. For each option, who is left without what they need, and by when does that cost fall due?
  4. Which document would you write first, what would you tell each of the other two on Friday, and what would you write next?

8. A note for the learner

This topic frames the choice by decision and audience rather than by habit. A document is a means of getting one reader to take one decision; each of the four common artefacts has a natural reader. A one-pager asks a busy person for a yes or no. A strategy document argues why a bet deserves resources. A PRD tells builders what to build and how they will know it is done. A spec fixes behaviour precisely enough to test. A well-reasoned answer names the decision that comes first, writes for that reader, and says plainly what the other readers will not yet have.

One defensible path is Option C, followed in sequence. The first decision in time is whether to start building at all, and the cheapest document that can carry it is the one-pager. It lets Hunjan and Hehar react to the same facts on the same day. With the remaining days Hothi could write the PRD for the funded slice only, and tell Hanjra the delivery window in writing, which is what the client's email asked for. The strategy document would follow for the board papers. Exhibit 3 has only three rows, so it cannot carry a causal claim, and the case for scope discipline does not rest on it. The path trades completeness for speed; Hehar would receive a slice of 8 engineer-weeks rather than 22, Hunjan less than a strategy document, and Dubai a window rather than a date; Hothi should say so in her covering note.

Pehel Technologies: Which Document, Which Audience

An Indian settlement-software company asks what it should have written down, the night before its board wants an answer.

I. Sunday night, 18 October 2026

At twenty past eleven on Sunday night, Bavleen Isher was still at her dining table in Indiranagar, Bengaluru, with two documents open and a third she had not started. The board of Pehel Technologies Private Limited met at nine the next morning in Pune, and the pre-read it asked for on Friday 2 October carried one line: what will change about how Pehel decides and records what it builds, and what will it cost. Tuesday was Dussehra, and half the Bengaluru floor would be away from Monday evening.

The two open documents were a 480-word one-pager published on Thursday 9 April, titled Deferred credit-note offsets, and a 4,900-word functional specification for the same part of the ledger, signed by a client's compliance officer in March and never updated. Between them, in a chat thread that no longer exists, sat the decision that cost Pehel ₹1.13 crore and put an ₹18.4 crore contract before a compliance committee on 30 November. Bavleen had been tagged in that thread; she had not replied.

Her own practice, announced on Monday 12 January 2026 in her third week as Vice-President, Product, was that a one-pager came first and a PRD was optional below a size threshold. Nine months on, Exhibit 1 counted 236 requirements documents in a single quarter. It was the third document — addressed to seven people who had read none of the others — that she could not begin.

II. The company, and the schedule that still binds it

Pehel was founded in Pune in 2021 by Balraj Issewal and two engineers from his previous employer, to solve the problem every Indian merchant with volume has: money arrives from a dozen rails — UPI through NPCI, cards, net banking, cash on delivery, marketplace payouts — and never in the shape the books expect. Pehel Settle reconciled the inflows, computed payouts and posted the result into a ledger finance teams could file from. In FY26, the year to 31 March 2026, revenue was ₹112 crore across 41 enterprise accounts, with 286 employees.

The decision that constrains Bavleen tonight was taken on 24 November 2023. To win Suvarnim Finserve Limited, a Chennai-headquartered non-banking financial company and Pehel's first regulated client, Balraj accepted Schedule 4 of the master services agreement: a signed functional specification for every release touching the lending ledger, signed by Suvarnim's compliance officer before deployment and retained seven years. In exchange Pehel got a three-year term, running from go-live, now worth ₹18.4 crore of annual recurring revenue.

In 2024 Pehel made a second decision, for good engineering reasons: one multi-tenant ledger for every customer rather than a lending ledger beside a merchant ledger. Schedule 4 was written for one module; the 2024 architecture made that module the floor of everything Pehel sells.

III. The industry

Pehel sells into the gap between the rails and the filing. Above it sit Oracle and SAP finance modules; below it Zoho's books and TallyPrime, adequate at low volume. Pehel's buyers are the tier between: a seller whose payouts arrive from Flipkart and Meesho on different cycles, a quick-commerce operator settling at Zepto's frequency, a lender collecting through Razorpay and PhonePe that must post the same day. Reserve Bank of India rules on recurring mandates changed what a settlement record must contain, GST e-invoicing pulled filing deadlines forward, ONDC multiplied a mid-sized seller's counterparties, and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 made a reconciliation file's contents a question of notice as well as arithmetic.

Pehel's second-largest account is outside India. Zamurrad Retail Group, headquartered in Dubai, runs stores across the UAE and Oman and pays ₹11.2 crore a year; with Suvarnim's ₹18.4 crore that is ₹29.6 crore of recurring revenue against FY26 revenue of ₹112 crore. Zamurrad bought because of the UAE's phased e-invoicing programme, which obliged it to net credit notes against subsequent settlements inside a VAT period. That requirement is what the 9 April one-pager described.

IV. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

Exhibit 4 draws the chain. On 9 April Bavleen's product manager for the Gulf accounts published the one-pager: Zamurrad needed credit notes netted inside a VAT period, and no PRD was required because the change sat below the 300-line threshold. On Tuesday 21 April, in a chat thread, Zamurrad's implementation manager asked for netting to continue across a period boundary when a credit note arrived late. Two of Bikramjeet Ichhra's leads agreed it was a one-line predicate change. Build began on Monday 4 May. Nobody re-opened the one-pager, and the acceptance criterion lived in a tracker comment.

Settle 3.11 reached Zamurrad's sandbox on Wednesday 3 June and production on Tuesday 23 June. The Zamurrad requirement was met and still is. But the predicate ran in the shared ledger, where an Indian merchant's period boundary is a GST return month, not a VAT quarter. For the June and July 2026 GST periods, ₹38 crore of settlements across 61,400 lines posted into the wrong period for twelve Indian merchants. A client's reconciliation of the June period flagged it on Wednesday 29 July; root cause was confirmed on Monday 17 August. Pehel paid ₹72 lakh in service credits and ₹41.09 lakh in rework.

Three things believed in August are no longer believed. First, that no document governed the change: the March specification covered the posting path and was accurate when signed. Second, that the chat thread would show who agreed to what; it has aged out of a 90-day retention, and what survives is a screenshot of four messages pasted into the one-pager's comments on 24 April. Third, that Suvarnim was unaffected: it lost nothing, but the release touched the shared ledger, so Schedule 4 applied and no signature existed. Exhibit 5 came from its compliance team on 6 October.

VIII. The options as Bavleen sees them tonight

Her working note lists five, in the order she first heard them.

A. The register. A mandatory PRD for every change above 300 changed lines, reviewed by a three-person artefact council with authority to hold a release. 118 of the 407 classified changes exceeded 300 lines, about 30 a quarter; at the Exhibit 2 medians of 14 author and 9 review hours that is 690 hours a quarter, ₹15.25 lakh at the all-role blended ₹2,210 from Exhibit 3, or ₹61 lakh a year. It is priced as if none of the 118 carries a PRD today, at the PRD row's full author and review hours. It leaves the chat channel and the tracker comment untouched.

B. The specification as contract. Move the Schedule 4 specification into the repository as a machine-checked API contract, with the signed PDF generated from it. Two platform engineers for two quarters, 1,920 hours at ₹1,950, is ₹37.44 lakh, and consumes both requisitions ring-fenced for the Zamurrad programme. It leaves the one-pager, the PRD and the strategy document as they are.

C. Audience first. Keep the one-pager for the squad, add a quarterly strategy document written for the board, and add a one-page change notice for client finance teams before every release that moves a posting rule. Schedule 4 stays as signed. The writing load moves to customer success (230 hours in Exhibit 3) and product marketing (absent from it), and the PRD disappears for unregulated work.

D. Buy the regime. A requirements and traceability suite, 45 seats at ₹7,000 a seat a month, ₹37.80 lakh a year, giving templates, an approval trail and an export an auditor can read. It leaves unchanged who decides scope.

E. Hire the writer. Two technical writers in Pune, fully loaded at ₹22 lakh each, ₹44 lakh a year, to draft and maintain specifications and change notices. It leaves the review time inside Exhibit 3's 3,562 hours where it is.

IX. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board meets at 09:00 on Monday 19 October. Suvarnim's compliance committee meets on 30 November and will decide whether 23 June was a Schedule 4 breach; the renewal, ₹18.4 crore, falls on Friday 15 January 2027, and Balraj has already signalled openness to liquidated damages. The process and tooling line is ₹95 lakh for the twelve months from 1 November 2026, so A and D together, at ₹98.80 lakh a year, do not fit it. Four requisitions are open and two are ring-fenced for Zamurrad. Schedule 4 cannot be renegotiated before January, and because of the 2024 single-ledger decision it reaches every posting rule Pehel ships. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act notice work is queued for Q4. Bhaswar's sabbatical starts on 1 December, and the Thursday review Baani no longer attends moves to a four-and-a-half-hour Berlin offset on 25 October.
